prompt: What is aggregate demand (AD)?

options.label: A
options.text: Output supplied at a given wage

options.label: B
options.text: Spending by households alone

options.label: C
options.text: Total spending at each price level

options.label: D
options.text: The economy’s stock of money balances at a particular date

explanation: Aggregate demand is total planned spending on the economy's goods and services at a given price level over a given period.

prompt: Which expression represents aggregate demand?

options.label: A
options.text: C + I + G + (X - M)

options.label: B
options.text: C + S + T + M

options.label: C
options.text: C + I + T + (M - X)

options.label: D
options.text: C + G + S + X

explanation: AD is made up of consumption, investment, government spending and net exports: C + I + G + (X - M).

prompt: In the aggregate demand identity, what does C represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Government purchases of additional equipment

options.label: B
options.text: Taxes on corporate income

options.label: C
options.text: Spending on goods imported by domestic consumers

options.label: D
options.text: Household consumption spending

explanation: C is consumption, also called consumer expenditure: spending by households on goods and services.

prompt: In the aggregate demand identity, what does I represent?

options.label: B
options.text: Purchases of products imported from overseas

options.label: C
options.text: Taxes levied indirectly on production

options.label: D

explanation: I is investment, meaning spending by private sector firms on capital goods.

prompt: In the aggregate demand identity, what does G represent?

options.label: B

prompt: What is aggregate supply (AS)?

options.label: A
options.text: Total output supplied at each price level

options.label: B
options.text: Planned spending by households

options.label: C
options.text: Output of one producing firm at its own selling price

options.label: D
options.text: Income set aside by households instead of being spent

explanation: Aggregate supply is total real output that producers in the economy are willing and able to supply at a given price level over a given period.

prompt: What is the main short-run feature used to distinguish SRAS from LRAS?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer prices remain permanently fixed during the short run.

options.label: B
options.text: Factor prices have not yet fully adjusted to changes.

options.label: C
options.text: All productive resources are fully employed in the short run.

options.label: D
options.text: Planned expenditure cannot change at all during the short run.

explanation: SRAS refers to a period in which input or factor prices have not fully adjusted to changes in aggregate demand and the price level.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.6 definition of Aggregate Supply (AS) | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is the main long-run feature used to distinguish LRAS from SRAS?

options.label: A
options.text: Factor prices have sufficient time to adjust fully.

options.label: B
options.text: Imports necessarily equal exports after sufficient time passes.

options.label: C
options.text: Government spending necessarily matches taxation after sufficient time passes.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer prices necessarily remain fixed after sufficient time passes.

explanation: LRAS refers to a period long enough for factor prices to adjust fully.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.6 definition of Aggregate Supply (AS) | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

options.label: C

options.label: D

prompt: Which effect helps explain why the AD curve slopes downward?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher prices increase the economy's stock of productive resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher prices reduce every firm's costs of productive inputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher prices expand the economy's long-run production possibilities frontier.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher prices reduce the purchasing power of financial wealth.

explanation: Under the wealth effect, a rise in the price level reduces the purchasing power of money balances and financial assets, reducing aggregate demand.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.4 shape of the AD curve (downward sloping) | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: How does the interest-rate effect help explain a downward-sloping AD curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher prices reduce interest rates and encourage only additional saving.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher prices increase productive capacity and the quantity of available resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower prices reduce export sales and encourage more imported consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher prices can raise interest rates and discourage interest-sensitive spending.

explanation: A higher price level increases the demand for money and can raise interest rates, which tends to reduce consumption and investment.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.4 shape of the AD curve (downward sloping) | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: How does the international effect help explain a downward-sloping AD curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher prices increase the available workforce

options.label: B
options.text: Lower prices increase firms’ unit costs across domestic industries

options.label: C
options.text: Higher prices raise productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Higher prices discourage exports and encourage imports

explanation: A higher domestic price level tends to reduce net exports because domestic products become less price competitive relative to foreign products.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.4 shape of the AD curve (downward sloping) | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

explanation: Lower consumption shifts AD left and higher productivity shifts SRAS right. Both lower the price level, while their output effects oppose one another.

prompt: Which shape is absent from both the classical vertical LRAS model and the three-section Keynesian LRAS model?

options.label: A
options.text: Vertical

options.label: B
options.text: Highly elastic on the initial section of the Keynesian curve

options.label: C
options.text: Upward sloping on the middle section of the Keynesian curve

options.label: D
options.text: Downward sloping

explanation: Classical LRAS is vertical at potential output. Three-section Keynesian aggregate supply contains a highly elastic section, an upward-sloping middle section and a vertical section near capacity. Neither model has a downward-sloping LRAS curve.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.8 shape of the AS curve in the short run and the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which change most directly shifts the vertical long-run aggregate supply curve to the right?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher consumer prices with productive resources unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater consumer confidence with productive resources unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater quantity or quality of productive resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower consumer prices with productive resources unchanged.

explanation: LRAS shifts right when productive potential rises through a greater quantity or better quality of resources.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.9 causes of a shift in the AS curve in the short run and in the long run | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: On the highly elastic section of a Keynesian LRAS curve, why can output increase with little price-level pressure?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy is at full capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Input prices rise proportionately with every increase in expenditure

options.label: C
options.text: Demand is unresponsive to consumer prices

options.label: D
options.text: Idle resources allow output to expand without large cost increases

explanation: When unemployment and spare capacity are high, firms can hire unused resources without causing large increases in factor prices.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.8 shape of the AS curve in the short run and the long run | AO2 Analysis

prompt: On the vertical section of a Keynesian LRAS curve, why does additional AD fail to raise real output?

options.label: A
options.text: Households stop making purchases when expenditure increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Existing resources are already at maximum sustainable capacity.

options.label: C
options.text: Imports must match exports when expenditure increases.

options.label: D
options.text: Firms face falling prices when expenditure increases.

explanation: At the vertical section, productive capacity is fully used, so extra aggregate demand can raise the price level but not sustainable real output.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.8 shape of the AS curve in the short run and the long run | AO2 Analysis

prompt: As an economy moves from the highly elastic toward the vertical section of a Keynesian LRAS curve, how does the effect of a given rightward AD shift typically change?

options.label: A
options.text: Output effects strengthen while price-level effects weaken.

options.label: B
options.text: Output effects weaken while price-level effects strengthen.

options.label: C
options.text: Both output effects and price-level effects disappear.

options.label: D
options.text: Price-level effects reverse while output effects strengthen.

explanation: As spare capacity diminishes, firms face increasing input constraints. Extra demand therefore generates less additional output and more price-level pressure.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.8; 4.3.12 shape of the AS curve in the short run and the long run; effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Two identical rightward AD shifts occur, first when output is low on a Keynesian LRAS curve and later near its vertical section. Which comparison is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Second shift: more output growth and less price pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: First shift: more output growth and less price pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Both shifts: identical output growth and identical price pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: First shift: lower output and lower price pressure.

explanation: The Keynesian shape implies more spare capacity at low output, so AD expansion has a stronger output effect and weaker price effect there.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.8; 4.3.12 shape of the AS curve in the short run and the long run; effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A rise in the general price level occurs with no change in any non-price determinant of demand or supply. Which combination of movements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A contraction along AD and an extension along SRAS

options.label: B
options.text: An extension along AD and a contraction along SRAS

options.label: C
options.text: A rightward shift of both AD and SRAS

options.label: D
options.text: A leftward shift of both AD and SRAS

explanation: A higher price level reduces the quantity of aggregate demand but increases the quantity of short-run aggregate supply along the existing curves.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.10 distinction between a movement along and a shift in AD and AS | AO2 Analysis

prompt: AD and SRAS both shift right, and the new equilibrium price level is higher. What can be inferred?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply's downward price effect dominates demand's upward price effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Real output falls as both curves move towards higher output.

options.label: C
options.text: Demand's upward price effect dominates supply's downward price effect.

options.label: D
options.text: One curve necessarily moved left rather than moving right.

explanation: Both shifts raise real output. AD expansion raises the price level while SRAS expansion lowers it, so a net price increase implies the AD price effect dominated.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.12 effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: AD and SRAS both shift right, and the new equilibrium price level is lower. What can be inferred?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply's downward price effect dominates demand's upward price effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Demand's upward price effect dominates supply's downward price effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Real output falls as both curves move towards higher output.

options.label: D
options.text: The two shifts necessarily have exactly equal output effects.

explanation: Both shifts increase real output. A net fall in the price level means the supply expansion's downward price effect dominated the demand expansion's upward effect.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.12 effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: AD shifts right and SRAS shifts left. The new equilibrium has higher real output. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply's negative output effect dominates demand's positive output effect.

options.label: B
options.text: The resulting price level necessarily falls below its original level.

options.label: C
options.text: Demand's positive output effect dominates supply's negative output effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Both curves must have moved right towards higher real output.

explanation: AD expansion raises output while SRAS contraction lowers it. Higher final output means the demand-side output effect dominated.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.12 effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: AD shifts right and SRAS shifts left. The new equilibrium has lower real output. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand's positive output effect dominates supply's negative output effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Supply's negative output effect dominates demand's positive output effect.

options.label: C
options.text: The resulting price level necessarily falls below its original level.

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate demand cannot have moved towards higher expenditure and output.

explanation: SRAS contraction lowers output while AD expansion raises it. A net output fall means the supply-side effect dominated.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.12 effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: AD shifts left and SRAS shifts right. The new equilibrium has higher real output. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand's negative output effect dominates supply's positive output effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Supply's positive output effect dominates demand's negative output effect.

options.label: C
options.text: The resulting price level necessarily rises above its original level.

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate supply cannot have moved towards higher output at each price.

explanation: AD contraction lowers output while SRAS expansion raises it. Higher final output means the supply expansion dominated the output effect.
reference: 4.3 Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply analysis | 4.3.12 effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: AD shifts left and SRAS shifts right. The new equilibrium has lower real output. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply's positive output effect dominates demand's negative output effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Demand's negative output effect dominates supply's positive output effect.

options.label: C
options.text: The resulting price level necessarily rises above its original level.

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate demand cannot have moved towards lower expenditure and output.

explanation: A leftward AD shift reduces output while a rightward SRAS shift increases it. A net fall means the AD effect dominated output.

prompt: Using a vertical LRAS curve, AD shifts right but productive capacity is unchanged. Which long-run outcome is consistent with the model?

options.label: B
options.text: Real output and the price level are both lower

options.label: C
options.text: Real output is unchanged and the price level is higher

options.label: D
options.text: Employment and output rise permanently beyond capacity

prompt: Advances in information technology raise productivity while household wealth also rises. What is most strongly supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Output falls; price level necessarily rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Price level rises; output effect is uncertain.

options.label: C
options.text: Output falls; price level necessarily falls.

options.label: D

explanation: Higher wealth raises AD, while better technology raises aggregate supply. Both effects increase real output, but they put opposite pressure on the price level.

prompt: Consumer confidence falls, raw material costs fall and productivity rises. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Prices rise; short-run output falls; productive capacity decreases.

options.label: B
options.text: Prices are uncertain; short-run output falls; productive capacity is unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Prices rise; short-run output rises; productive capacity decreases.

options.label: D
options.text: Prices fall; short-run output is uncertain; productive capacity increases.

explanation: Lower confidence shifts AD left. Lower raw material costs and higher productivity shift SRAS right, so all three changes put downward pressure on the price level. AD contraction lowers output while supply expansion raises it, making the short-run output effect uncertain. Higher productivity also shifts LRAS right, increasing productive capacity.

prompt: An economy experiences a rise in incomes in its main export markets and, at the same time, a temporary natural disaster disrupts domestic production. Which combination of curve shifts is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: AD shifts left and SRAS shifts right

options.label: B
options.text: Both AD and SRAS shift right

options.label: C
options.text: AD shifts right and SRAS shifts left

options.label: D
options.text: Neither curve shifts because both changes affect only the price level

explanation: Higher incomes abroad are likely to increase demand for the economy's exports, raising net exports and shifting AD to the right. A temporary natural disaster can reduce the quantity of resources available for current production, shifting SRAS to the left.
